item.title: Bilateral Agreements III: The Council of States Calls for a Referendum
item.description: The Council of States voted 23 to 17, with 3 abstentions, in favor of a mandatory referendum on the Bilateral Agreements III. The matter now goes to the National Council.
item.content:encoded:
## In Brief - The cantons are calling for a mandatory referendum on the Bilateral Agreements III - The vote ended 23 to 17, with 3 abstentions - Now it’s up to the National Council - Cassis believes the goal is still achievable
- Subject → new package of bilateral agreements with the European Union - Decision → mandatory referendum - Outcome → 23 votes in favor, 17 against, and 3 abstentions - Required majority → the people and the cantons - Next step → debate in the National Council - Federal Government’s position → optional referendum on international treaties
With 23 votes in favor, 17 against, and 3 abstentions, the Council of States has called for the new package of bilateral agreements with the European Union to be subject to a mandatory referendum. The consequence outlined in the debate is clear: approval would require a double majority—from both the people and the cantons.
The matter must now be debated by the National Council. The referral to the Council of States therefore does not mark the end of the process for Bilateral Agreements III. In the meantime, however, the Council of States has rebuked the Federal Government, which had repeatedly expressed support for an optional referendum on international treaties.
The Council of States’ vote thus contains two political signals. On the one hand, it establishes the requirement for a mandatory referendum on the package; on the other, it opens a path that will need to be evaluated by the National Council. The debate in the National Council has yet to take place.
### Cassis’s Assessment
In an interview with RSI, Ignazio Cassis, Federal Councilor and head of the Federal Department of Foreign Affairs, described the result as “more glass half-full than half-empty.” He acknowledged that the outcome does not exactly match what the Federal Council had hoped for, but he framed the vote within the broader discussion on the balance between democracy and federalism.
> “It’s more full than empty.”
Cassis also described the six-hour debate in the Council of States as high-quality, arguing that the discussion delved deeply into the very foundations of the Confederation and the state. On the political merits, the head of the FDFA believes that the Bilateral Agreements III remain on the right track. In his view, the cantons largely followed the Federal Council’s lead, while adding some of their own emphasis.
As for the double referendum, Cassis argued that it would not significantly affect the chances of the package being approved. He did, however, acknowledge the need for significant effort to explain and clarify the rationale behind Bilateral Agreements III, describing the goal as achievable. The practical significance of the cantonal vote can be seen in the difference between the two paths compared in the debate: the one supported by the Federal Government, oriented toward an optional referendum, and the one approved by the Council of States, which calls for a mandatory referendum. The second formula explicitly links the package to a double majority, of both the people and the cantons.
For those living in Switzerland, the point to follow is therefore the electorate that must be convinced. Cassis does not describe the additional requirement as an automatic obstacle: he argues that Bilaterals III can be accepted by the people and the cantons. But he acknowledges that the explanation of the package will have to be broader and capable of clarifying why the choice was made.
### A step that requires listening to the regions
The call for listening to the regions emerges above all when the head of the DFAE speaks about the small cantons. According to Cassis, it will be necessary to go to the small cantons that feel somewhat distant from these discussions, because they have no industries and have needs that are entirely different from those of major industrial centers such as Zurich, the Léman Arc or eastern Switzerland, with reference to the Rhine Valley.
This distinction makes the debate less uniform. The same proposal must be presented to cantonal communities that, according to Cassis's description, do not share the needs of the major industrial areas. For the reader, this means observing not only the content of the package, but also how the Federal Council intends to present it in the different cantons.
The opposition of the UDC emerged in the debate, along with that of part of the Centre and the PLR. Cassis does not challenge the legitimacy of these positions: he recalls that these are elected people who are entitled to express them consistently and clearly. The political fact, however, cannot automatically be carried over to the next stage. According to the federal councillor, the dynamic will be very different in the National Council, because the interplay of the cantons and federalism weighed heavily in the Council of States.

### A Step-by-Step Guide
1. Identify the subject of the decision: The Council of States has called for a mandatory referendum on the new package of bilateral agreements with the European Union.

item.title: Swiss Oppose Taxes on Sugar, Salt, or Fats
item.description: 68% of those surveyed by Gfs.Bern reject the tax on food. The monitoring highlights calls for prevention and the protection of minors.
item.content:encoded:
## At a Glance - 68% oppose taxes on sugar, salt, or fats - 76% consider measures against obesity insufficient - 89% support mandatory nutrition education in schools - 82% approve of a ban on advertising to children under 13
## Key Facts Sample → over 1,000 respondents Period → between March and May Research firm → Gfs.Bern Survey → 13th edition Source → Keystone-ATS Food tax → 68% opposed Tax to fund nutrition education → 45% in favor Minimum age for sugary foods → 19% in favor
68% of the more than 1,000 respondents surveyed between March and May by Gfs.Bern say they oppose a tax on foods containing sugar, salt, or fat. The data comes from the 13th edition of a survey sponsored by the Soft Drink Information Group, an organization founded in 2013 by industry producers that includes representatives from the political and business worlds.
Keystone-ATS reports that the Swiss public wants the government to play a more active role in combating obesity, but without new taxes or bans. The survey indicates a preference for individual responsibility, accompanied by a call for greater protection of children from advertising.
The findings therefore address both the role of the government and the choice of tools for intervention. The survey distinguishes between tax measures and measures focused on prevention, education, and advertising. Public opinion varies significantly among these options.
### The Vote on the Proposals
Opposition to the tax is also driven by the fear that the levy would place a greater burden on the poorest people and would not change eating habits. The proposal to tax the same products to fund public information campaigns garners 45% support and thus fails to secure a majority. Support for a minimum age requirement to purchase sugary foods is even lower: 19% of respondents support this idea, making it the least popular option.
### Prevention and Minors
76% of the sample believes that the measures taken so far to prevent obesity are insufficient. 90% supports prevention programs for at-risk groups and joint initiatives with the private sector. Eighty-nine percent support mandatory nutrition education in schools. Eighty-two percent also support a ban on advertising foods containing sugar, salt, or fat that is targeted at children under 13.
Food manufacturers are working with the federal government to develop a voluntary commitment plan. This monitoring effort thus complements support for more active government intervention with a focus on individual responsibility, prevention, education, child protection, and collaboration with the private sector. The survey offers a practical way to interpret the findings: not all proposals to combat obesity affect the same aspect of daily life. The tax on foods containing sugar, salt, or fat affects purchasing decisions; nutrition education focuses on schools; advertising targets children under 13; prevention programs target at-risk groups. Joint initiatives, on the other hand, involve the economy. This distinction clarifies a result that would otherwise seem contradictory: the government should do more, but the preferred approach does not necessarily involve a new tax or a restriction on purchases.
### A Map of Options
| Plan | Measure Described | Point to Consider | |---|---|---| | Purchases | Tax on sugar, salt, or fat | The potential burden on the poorest people and the effect on eating habits | | Information | Tax earmarked to fund public information campaigns | Support remains below a majority | | Schools | Mandatory teaching of nutrition principles | The role assigned to schools | | Minors | Ban on advertising to children under 13 | Protecting children as a goal | | Prevention | Programs for at-risk groups and projects with the private sector | The involvement of various stakeholders |
The table shows that the debate is not merely about whether or not to support public intervention. It also concerns who should be involved and which measures are considered acceptable. Individual responsibility remains the starting point indicated by the survey, while prevention, schools, and protection from advertising receive support.
For those living in Switzerland, the difference is clear in practice: a tax proposal is judged based on its impact on the poorest people; school-based or advertising interventions focus on specific target groups; joint initiatives create a role for the private sector. The voluntary commitment plan that food producers are developing with the federal government adds a distinct channel separate from the tax and the minimum age requirement.
If these preferences were to guide future decisions, the focus would thus shift toward prevention, education, child protection, and collaboration, without negating individual responsibility. This is a scenario derived from the survey data; the text, however, describes a voluntary plan currently being developed by food producers and the Swiss Confederation.

item.title: Parental Leave: 112,517 signatures in support of 18 weeks
item.description: In Bern, 112'517 signatures were submitted calling for 18 weeks of parental leave for both mothers and fathers.
item.content:encoded:
## At a Glance - 112,517 certified signatures submitted in Bern - 18 weeks for each parent under the proposal - Currently: 14 weeks for mothers, 2 for fathers - 100,000 signatures are needed within 18 months
## Key Facts - Date → September 30, 2026 - Location → Federal Chancellery, Bern - Signatures → 112,517 certified - Proposal → 18 weeks for both mothers and fathers - Threshold → 100,000 signatures within 18 months - Mothers today → 14 weeks - Fathers today → 2 weeks starting in 2021
On September 30, 2026, in Bern, the initiative’s sponsors submitted 112,517 certified signatures to the Federal Chancellery for the popular initiative calling for 18 weeks of parental leave for each parent. The signature drive has thus formally succeeded: a popular initiative requires 100,000 signatures within 18 months of the text’s official publication in the Federal Gazette.
The proposed constitutional amendment is titled “A Strong Society and Economy Thanks to Parental Leave” (Family Leave Initiative). The text refers to “equitable and compensated” parental leave upon the birth of a child, with the same duration for mothers and fathers. For details on the measure, consult the guide on congedo parentale; however, keep in mind that this proposal differs from the rules currently in place in Switzerland.
### Proposed Support and Rules
The initiative is supported by representatives from the Center Party, the Greens, the PVL, the PS, the PEV, and the PLR, as well as by Alliance F and Travail.Suisse. The text sets out certain criteria regarding duration, usage, and compensation.
According to the proposal, the leave should not be transferable from one parent to the other. In principle, both parents could take it simultaneously for up to one-quarter of the total duration. The minimum amount and the funding of the allowance should follow the principles applied to allowances for those performing military or civilian service. For lower wages, the allowance should increase progressively until it reaches 100%.
The proposal also takes the current situation into account. Working mothers are currently entitled to 14 weeks of maternity benefits. In 2020, voters approved two weeks of paternity leave, which took effect in early 2021. The proposed bill therefore suggests an equal duration of 18 weeks for both parents, whereas the legislation cited in the source provides for different periods. ## From the Current Situation to the Proposal
For those who work and are about to become parents, the issue is not just about the number of weeks. The bill places the required duration for mothers and fathers on an equal footing, stipulates that parental leave should not be transferable, and, in principle, limits simultaneous use. These are the three key points to consider when comparing the current framework to the proposed bill.
### Equality and Organization of Parental Leave
| Group | Today, according to the source | Proposal | |---|---|---| | Mothers | 14 weeks of maternity benefits | 18 weeks | | Fathers | 2 weeks of leave, effective as of early 2021 | 18 weeks |
The most obvious difference is the equal duration. The text does not simply call for adding a period of leave for fathers: it calls for each parent to have 18 weeks. For mothers, the proposal compares with the 14 weeks of maternity leave currently in effect; for fathers, with the two weeks that took effect in 2021.
The non-transferability shifts the focus from the family’s total duration of leave to the situation of each parent. If the proposal were adopted as described, the weeks allocated to one parent could not be transferred to the other. This rule is accompanied by a restriction on simultaneous use: in principle, the two parents could take leave together for only one-quarter of the total duration. The text, therefore, combines individual equality with only partial shared use.
### Benefits and Wages
The second section concerns the economic value of the leave. The initiative links the minimum amount and the funding of the benefit to the principles applied to benefits for those performing military or civil service. For the lowest wages, the amount should increase progressively up to 100%. The reference to 100% does not describe an identical amount for everyone: it indicates the target set for the allowance intended for the lowest wages.
To understand the comparison without confusing duration and financial support, consult the guide on congedo parentale. Meanwhile, the source keeps the current framework distinct from the constitutional amendment requested by the proponents.

The news can be read in a practical step-by-step manner, without confusing the signature drive with the content of the leave policy. This method helps distinguish between what the source describes as the current law and what the proponents are requesting in the constitutional amendment.
1. Start with the current situation. Note the 14 weeks of maternity leave for working mothers and the two weeks for fathers, which were approved in 2020 and took effect in early 2021. 2. Isolate the proposal. List the 18 weeks for each parent on a separate line. This is the duration requested in the text, distinct from the one described as the current situation. 3. Review the structure. Verify that the text refers to non-transferable leave and simultaneous use, generally limited to one-quarter of the total duration. 4. Read the financial section. Look for the two criteria mentioned: the principles governing allowances for military or civilian service—specifically the minimum amount and funding—and a progressive increase up to 100% for the lowest wages. 5. File the petition. The threshold is 100,000 signatures within 18 months of the text’s official publication in the Federal Gazette. The submitted petition consists of 112,517 signatures certified by the Federal Chancellery.
### Dates Not to Be Confused
September 30, 2026, marks the date of submission to Bern. The years 2020 and early 2021, however, pertain to the paternity leave currently under discussion. The 18-month period refers to the signature-gathering phase, while the 18-week period refers to the duration of leave requested by each parent. Distinguishing these dates prevents the end of the signature-gathering period from being misinterpreted as the duration of the entitlement.

item.title: Drought and heatwave: the debate in the National Council
item.description: The National Council is debating twelve parliamentary questions on the drought. Rösti announces a new water strategy for next year.
item.content:encoded:
## At a Glance - The National Council discussed twelve urgent interpellations - Rösti announces a water strategy for next year - Water, health, and agriculture at the center of the debate
## Key Facts - Location → Bern - Topic → heat wave and drought - Interpellations → twelve, addressed to DETEC - Next step → new water management strategy - Sectors → water, vulnerable populations, and agriculture
Bern hosted the National Council’s current affairs debate on heat waves and drought. The twelve urgent parliamentary questions addressed to the Federal Department of the Environment, Transportation, Energy, and Communications brought three related issues to the floor: water shortages, protecting vulnerable populations from heat waves, and measures to support agriculture.
The debate brought together a variety of demands. The Liberal Greens called for a national water management strategy and greater protection of buildings. Corina Gredig (PVL/ZH) pointed to the need to increase water reserves. The Greens criticized Albert Rösti, head of DATEC, for expressing surprise at the severity of the drought.
### The Groups’ Positions
Franziska Ryser (SG) brought the health issue to the forefront of the debate:
> The heat wave is not just a nuisance, but also a health hazard.
Speaking for the Socialists, Mattea Meyer (ZH) asked why there is no action plan for the period 2026–2030. From the Center Party, Stefan Müller-Altermatt (SO) warned of the possible consequences of the drought on agriculture in the coming years. Christian Wasserfallen (PLR/BE), on the other hand, advocated for greater use of modern technologies and adaptation measures, especially for workers.
### Government, Municipalities, and Energy
The SVP defended the actions of its minister. Ernst Wandfluh (BE) praised the speed with which the government adopted measures during the crisis, including the exemption from customs duties on animal feed and the forest health subsidy.
Rösti said he wanted to support cantons and municipalities in their areas of responsibility, citing the climate control of public buildings and the management of reservoirs. For the latter area, he intends to propose a new strategy next year. On nuclear power, he explained that this source is particularly useful in winter, while solar power’s contribution increases in summer. Decarbonization, he added, remains the top priority. The practical value of the debate lies in the distinction between levels of intervention. Water management is not presented as solely an agricultural issue: the concerns extend to reserves, reservoirs, real estate, and public health. For those who live or work in Switzerland, this broadens the scope of the decisions to be made: the DATEC remains the focal point of the national discussion, while cantons and municipalities come into play regarding public buildings and reservoirs.
The most concrete step for local communities is therefore the combination of coordination and local expertise. The national strategy called for by the Liberal Greens and the one that Rösti intends to propose next year outline a general framework; air conditioning in public buildings and the management of reservoirs, on the other hand, fall under the purview of cantons and municipalities. For the reader, this distinction helps avoid confusing a national policy direction with a measure already implemented everywhere.

In agriculture, the debate compares different time frames. The Center focuses on the consequences in the coming years; the SVP, on the other hand, emphasizes measures adopted quickly during the crisis. The key for the sector is to consider both the immediate response and the long-term risk together, without confusing a measure mentioned in the chamber with a new strategy already in place.

item.title: Analysts Less Optimistic About the Swiss Economy
item.description: In September, the Swiss economic outlook index stood at +2.6 points, down 9.5 points from August, according to UBS and CFA Society Switzerland.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - September index: +2,6 points, 9,5 lower than August. - 23,1% see an improvement over the next six months. - 56,4% expect an unchanged situation. - UBS and CFA Society Switzerland: 78 analysts.
## Key facts - Indicator → +2,6 points - Comparison with August → decrease of 9,5 points - Sample → 78 analysts - Survey dates → 17 and 24 September - Horizon → next six months - Calculation → 23,1% minus 20,5% = +2,6 points - Partner through 2023 → Credit Suisse - Current partner → UBS
In September, the index on the prospects for the Swiss economy stood at +2,6 points, down 9,5 points from August. The figure is still positive, but financial analysts' optimism about the evolution of the Swiss business cycle has declined.
The indicator is calculated by UBS and CFA Society Switzerland based on a survey of experts. The launch is attributed to Keystone-ATS; the acronym ATS is given in the news reference. The survey was conducted on 17 and 24 September, with the participation of 78 analysts from the Swiss financial community.
### The balance between confidence and caution
23,1% of respondents expect an improvement in economic conditions over the next six months. 20,5% instead expect a deterioration, while 56,4% expect no changes. These three shares make up the main index: 23,1% minus 20,5% gives +2,6 points.
Comparison with August shows a less favorable movement. Optimists decreased by 7,2 points; pessimists increased by 2,3 points and the group expecting the status quo grew by 4,9 points. The largest share therefore remains that of those expecting stability, while the overall balance remains in positive territory.
By construction, the balance compares those expecting an improvement with those expecting a deterioration. Those indicating stability neither increase nor reduce the arithmetic value, but explain why a positive index can coexist with a majority oriented toward the status quo.
The survey has been conducted since January 2017. Until 2023, CFA's partner was Credit Suisse. CFA is described in the source as an association of investment professionals with American roots; the partner is now UBS, the bank that acquired the competitor. September's result thus captures expectations that are still positive, but less broad than in the previous month. ## Prices, Rates, and Markets
The picture becomes more nuanced when looking at inflation, interest rates, the SMI, exchange rates, and unemployment. For those who live or work in Switzerland, the practical value lies in comparing expected trends, without turning the survey into a personal figure to apply to one’s own budget.
### Expected Trends
Regarding inflation, 48.7% of the sample expects inflation in Switzerland to rise, 5.1% expects it to fall, and 46.2% expects it to remain stable. This distribution indicates which scenario is most widely held among analysts but does not assign a numerical value to inflation. The data should therefore be interpreted as an indication of trends, not as a measure of price changes for an individual household.
Regarding interest rates, stability prevails in the short term at 61.3%, while 36% expect a rise. In the long term, the largest group—48%—sees no changes, while 41.3% expect an increase. Stability remains the leading forecast for both time horizons, but the expectation of a rise retains a significant presence in the responses.
The stock market also sends a clear signal. 53.5% of respondents expect the SMI index to rise over the next six months, an increase of 4.0 percentage points compared to August. 31% anticipate stable levels, and 15.5% expect a decline. This indication pertains to the SMI and does not automatically correspond to the general assessment of the economic situation.
### Exchange Rates and Employment
Regarding the franc against the euro, 44.6% expect it to strengthen, 18.9% expect it to weaken, and 36.5% expect no change. Against the dollar, the percentages are 44.6%, 18.9%, and 29.7%, in that order. The difference therefore lies primarily in the proportion of those expecting stability. For a practical comparison between the franc and the euro, the comparatore CHF/EUR can be used.
Regarding unemployment, 38.7% expect the number of unemployed to rise, 58.7% expect it to remain stable, and 2.7% expect it to fall. Again, these are analysts’ expectations, not individual counts. The survey results can be used as a framework for interpretation, provided you keep three key points in mind: the survey date, the time horizon, and the projected direction. Following a simple procedure helps avoid confusing an aggregate expectation with an outcome that has already been observed.
### Four Practical Steps
1. Define the time frame: note September 17 and 24, the survey dates, along with the 78 responses from the Swiss financial community. The sample defines who is expressing the expectation.
2. Separate the time horizons: use the next six months for the economic outlook and the SMI; for interest rate expectations, distinguish between the short and long term. Do not treat different time intervals as equivalent.
3. Record the direction for each item: improvement, deterioration, or stability for the economic outlook; increase, decrease, or stability for inflation, the stock market, exchange rates, and unemployment. The categories retain their original meanings.
4. Keep the euro and the dollar separate: for the franc, note the three percentages relative to the euro and then those relative to the dollar. For operational comparison, use comparatore CHF/EUR.
The next step is to examine the largest group together with the minority shares. A predominance of stability does not negate the portion of the sample that sees an increase, a decline, or a contraction. Similarly, a majority on one indicator does not automatically describe the others.

item.title: Health Insurance Premiums: When 3.7% Doesn't Tell the Whole Story
item.description: In 2027, the average health insurance premium in Ticino will increase by 3,7%, reaching 519.90 francs per month, an increase of 18.60 francs, 26% higher than the Swiss average of 412 francs.
item.content:encoded:
## At a Glance - In 2027, the average premium in Ticino will rise by 3.7%. - The Swiss average will increase by 5%. - Ticino residents will pay 519.90 francs per month. - The premium in Ticino will be 26% above the national average.
## Key Facts - Period → 2027 - Ticino → average increase of 3.7% - Swiss average → average increase of 5% - Average premium in Ticino → from 501.30 to 519.90 francs per month - Monthly increase → 18.60 francs - Rank by increase in francs → 13th out of 26 cantons - Swiss average premium → 412 francs per month - Median salary → 5,708 francs in Ticino compared to 7,024 francs for the national average
For 2027, the average health insurance premium in Ticino is projected to rise by 3.7%. This percentage is below 5% of the Swiss average and comes on the heels of the steep increases of recent years. The initial sign is positive: Ticino appears to be among the cantons least affected.
Glarus recorded a 3% increase, while Vaud saw a 3.5% rise. These are the only cantons with a lower percentage increase than Ticino’s. However, the picture changes when the percentage is converted into francs—that is, the actual amount that comes out of policyholders’ pockets each month.
### The Ranking in Francs
The average premium in Ticino rises from 501.30 to 519.90 francs per month. The increase is 18.60 francs. When compared with the other cantons, Ticino no longer ranks third among those with the smallest increase: it now ranks 13th out of 26 cantons. The difference between the two rankings is not a contradiction, but the result of a percentage applied to an already high baseline.
The gap becomes even clearer when compared to the national average. In 2027, the average premium in Ticino will reach 519.90 francs per month, compared to the Swiss average of 412 francs. The gap is 107.90 francs per month, equal to 1,294.80 francs per year for each insured person. The premium in Ticino will therefore be about 26% higher than the national average.
Lorenzo Onderka, a supporter of “Avanti con Ticino&Lavoro,” compares these figures with those from the Federal Statistical Office (UST/BFS). The latest data show a median wage of 5,708 francs in Ticino—the lowest among Switzerland’s major regions—compared to the national average of 7,024 francs. The key point is not to deny the slowdown, but to measure it alongside actual spending: the percentage describes growth, while the amount in francs shows the impact on the monthly budget. To view comparisons with other tools on this topic, the reference remains cassa malati. ## When a Percentage Isn’t Enough
Comparing percentages and francs changes how the announcement is interpreted. A percentage measures the rate of increase; the monthly amount shows how much of a burden it places on the budget. In the case of Ticino, the 3.7% increase is applied to an average premium that is already high. That is why the increase amounts to 18.60 francs per month, even though the percentage increase remains lower than the national average.
### The Growing Gap
The practical issue is the difference compared to the Swiss average. The average premium for policyholders in Ticino is 519.90 francs per month, compared to 412 francs. The monthly gap of 107.90 francs amounts to 1,294.80 francs over the course of a year. For a couple, the source estimates the impact at nearly 2,600 francs annually. This is not an abstract figure: these are resources that could be diverted from other necessities, consumption, or savings.
Comparing this to income figures makes the situation clearer. Ticino’s median wage of 5,708 francs is cited as the lowest among Switzerland’s major regions, while the national average is 7,024 francs. The average health insurance premium in Ticino, on the other hand, is about 26% above the Swiss average. The combination described by the source is therefore twofold: a higher monthly cost and a lower median wage.
This does not negate the slowdown. In 2025, the increase in healthcare costs in Ticino was below the national average, and the measures taken may be starting to yield results. This finding remains to be acknowledged, but it does not replace the question regarding the starting point. Even more modest growth can still exert significant pressure when the base premium is already high.
To relate premium spending to daily out-of-pocket expenses, one can refer to costo della vita in Svizzera, without confusing the improvement in the percentage with a reduction in the gap in francs.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the net salary calculator and the CHF-EUR exchange comparator. ## From Percentages to the Budget: A Practical Guide
To analyze an advertisement without focusing solely on the percentage, you can follow a four-step process. There’s no need to choose between percentages and francs: both measures are necessary, as the author argues.
### Four Steps to Analyzing the Advertisement
1. Identify the reference point. Separate the average increase in Ticino (3.7%) from the Swiss average (5%). Also keep the figures for Glarus (3%) and Vaud (3.5%) distinct: these are percentage comparisons, not monthly amounts.
2. Convert the rate to francs. Pair the 3.7% figure with the increase from 501.30 to 519.90 francs per month. The figure to focus on is therefore 18.60 francs per month. This adjustment prevents a ranking based solely on percentages from obscuring Ticino’s position, which, in francs, ranks 13th out of 26 cantons.
3. Extend the comparison to a full year. Use the difference from the Swiss average: 107.90 francs per month and 1,294.80 francs per year for each insured person. For a couple, the figure is nearly 2,600 francs. This is the measure that most closely reflects the impact on household finances.
4. Consider income alongside premiums. Examine the premium in relation to the median income: 5,708 francs in Ticino versus 7,024 francs for the national average. This comparison is not meant to replace the premium data but to illustrate its relative impact on household budgets.
The same table also allows you to view the 2025 data: the increase in healthcare costs in Ticino was below the national average. This slowdown should be noted without overlooking the starting point. In public communications, percentages and amounts should therefore appear in the same context.
To accompany the comparison with disposable income, use calcolatore stipendio. For the specific topic of LAMal/KVG premiums, consult guide cassa malati.

item.title: 2027 Budget: Unions challenge austerity and the rising cost of living
item.description: OCST, VPOD, and SIT are challenging the State Council’s 2027 Budget Proposal, calling for a “change of course.” They criticize the 0.25% cost-of-living adjustment and the failure to replace 10% of the staff.
item.content:encoded:
## In Brief - OCST, VPOD, and SIT are calling for a “change of course” - The cost-of-living adjustment for staff is set at 0.25% - 10% of departing staff would not be replaced - Criticism also directed at USI, SUPSI, and public schools
## Key Facts - Subject → 2027 Budget - Unions → OCST, VPOD, and SIT - Cost-of-living adjustment → 0.25% for cantonal staff - Departing staff → 10% will not be replaced - Contributions → USI and SUPSI - Related content → 3.7% increase in health insurance premiums in Ticino in 2027
OCST, VPOD, and SIT are challenging the cost-cutting measures contained in the 2027 Budget presented by the State Council. The three unions are calling on the government and parliament to “change course,” abandon the cuts, and guarantee full compensation for inflation.
The unions reserve the right to conduct a more in-depth analysis of the budget, but they already view the document as a continuation of the spending restraint policy of previous years. Their criticism centers on the potential impact on public services and working conditions.
### The Contested Points
The first area highlighted is the social and health care sector. Funding would be reduced while, according to the unions, the need for care continues to rise. For subsidized organizations, the reduction in funding would limit their ability to adjust staffing levels and services. The feared result is increased pressure on staff and greater difficulty in ensuring care.
A second issue concerns the failure to replace 10% of departing staff. This measure has already been approved by the Grand Council over a three-year period. However, OCST, VPOD, and SIT object to an implementation that does not take into account the needs of individual services: in their view, workloads would increase and staff conditions would worsen.
The budget also provides for a 0.25% cost-of-living adjustment for cantonal staff, with knock-on effects for various subsidized employers. For the labor unions, this percentage is insufficient given the projected inflation rate and does not make up for what was not granted in previous years. The demand therefore also includes compensation for past inflation, to prevent a further loss of purchasing power. This issue directly affects costo della vita in Svizzera, though it remains subject to a cantonal decision.
Other measures cited include reduced contributions to USI and SUPSI, cuts to the Red Cross, a lack of investment in public schools, and a reduction in staffing at the Police Academy. The unions are also looking ahead to the coming years and calling for greater investment in public and quasi-public services, with funding commensurate with the needs of the population. ## What This Means for Workers
The text links three factors that, in practice, have different effects: funding for organizations, staffing levels, and adjustments for the cost of living. Reading each item in isolation risks missing the connection highlighted by OCST, VPOD, and SIT. Reduced funding may limit the ability of subsidized agencies to adjust staffing levels and services; staff replacements implemented without considering individual services may increase workloads; and a 0.25% adjustment may not fully offset past inflation, according to the unions.
### The Before-and-After Comparison
The comparison with previous years primarily concerns the continuation of the spending restraint policy and the failure to compensate for inflation. The 2027 Budget proposes a 0.25% increase, while the unions are demanding full compensation, including for past inflation. The key point to note, therefore, is not just the nominal increase: it is the gap between what is projected and what the unions deem necessary to prevent a further loss of purchasing power. For cantonal employees—and for various subsidized employers—this change can also be tracked on their own busta paga svizzera form, without converting the percentage figure into amounts not specified in the source.
The timing should also be viewed from two perspectives. The decision not to replace 10% of departing staff is a measure already approved by the Grand Council to be implemented over three years; the objection concerns the risk that its implementation may not take into account the needs of individual departments. Separating the decision from its implementation helps explain why the unions are focusing on workloads and staff conditions—not just cost savings.
### A Figure Not to Be Confused
The 3.7% mentioned in a related headline refers to the increase in health insurance premiums in Ticino for 2027. This is not the 0.25% cost-of-living increase projected in the budget: the first figure pertains to health insurance funds, while the second concerns cantonal staff and, by extension, various subsidized employers. Making this distinction prevents the addition of two percentages referring to different issues and allows for a correct interpretation of the comparison regarding the cost of living.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the net salary calculator and the CHF-EUR exchange comparator. ## How to Review the Report
To turn the 2027 Budget Proposal into a concrete analysis, it is best to follow a simple sequence and stick to the categories listed in the source.
### Four Key Areas
1. Start with the document presented by the State Council and divide your review into four areas: social and health care, personnel, cost of living, and other contributions or investments. The last area includes USI and SUPSI, the Red Cross, public schools, and the Police Academy.
2. Separate budgetary measures from decisions that have already been adopted. The decision not to replace 10% of departing staff was approved by the Grand Council over a three-year period. The key point to monitor is therefore its implementation within individual departments, which the unions are asking not to be handled without considering specific needs.
3. Consider the 0.25% figure in conjunction with the request for full compensation for inflation, including past inflation. This figure applies to cantonal staff and, by extension, to various subsidized employers.
4. Distinguish this issue from the related matter of health insurance funds: the 3.7% figure indicated for 2027 in Ticino is not the cost-of-living adjustment percentage in the budget. Keeping the two plans separate avoids confusion regarding the cost of living.
The political development to monitor is the debate requested by the unions from the government and parliament. Their message is to abandon cuts in the social and health care sectors and the non-replacement of some staff, increase investment in public and quasi-public services, and align funding with the needs of the population. The same unions have reserved the right to conduct a more in-depth analysis of the budget: this is the step recommended by the source for evaluating individual measures.
To track the impact on personal income and understand the components of a Swiss salary, use calcolatore stipendio.

item.title: Swiss watchmaking: luxury alone is not enough
item.description: Deloitte expert Karine Szegedi warns: declining sales volumes and a focus on luxury are putting nearly 700 companies at risk. The 1,000–3,000 franc price range is being neglected, while the price-performance ratio is crucial.
item.content:encoded:
## At a Glance - Sales volumes have declined significantly. - Luxury alone cannot sustain nearly 700 watch companies. - Value for money is the primary criterion in 12 out of 13 markets. - Country of origin is the primary criterion for 15%, down from 20% in 2022.
## Key Facts - Warning → Karine Szegedi, industry expert at Deloitte - Source → interview published by the Neue Zürcher Zeitung (NZZ) - Industrial base → nearly 700 watchmaking companies - Neglected price range → between 1,000 and 3,000 francs - Country of origin → primary criterion for 15% in 13 key markets - Comparison → 20% in 2022 - Main criterion → price-performance ratio in 12 out of 13 markets - Opportunities → India and the women’s market
### The warning about the watchmaking industry Nearly 700 watchmaking companies make up the watchmaking industry, which, according to Karine Szegedi, would risk not being sustained if Switzerland were to produce almost exclusively luxury watches. The industry expert at Deloitte sounded the alarm today in an interview published by the Neue Zürcher Zeitung (NZZ). The news was reported by Keystone-ATS.
The argument stems from the question: sales volumes have declined significantly and are unlikely to return to previous levels. The decline primarily affects suppliers of movements, dials, cases, and other components, who depend more on production volumes than the brands themselves. They require a certain level of plant utilization to maintain and develop machinery, skilled labor, and know-how.
The shift toward the high-end market, Szegedi notes, is understandable. Swiss wage levels, the strong franc, rising gold prices, and stringent production requirements make manufacturing costly. However, Switzerland possesses extensive expertise in complicated watches and specialized craftsmanship; international collectors are willing to pay a premium. Many manufacturers therefore focus on complicated watches with elaborate designs.
### The Untapped Segment According to the expert, this approach neglects the price range between 1,000 and 3,000 francs, where there are currently relatively few Swiss manufacturers. This is an important entry-level segment for mechanical watches. In less mature markets such as India or Mexico—and even in the United States—more Swiss offerings could boost sales.
Meanwhile, country of origin is cited as the most important purchasing criterion by 15% of respondents in 13 key markets, down from 20% in 2022. Value for money is the primary criterion in 12 of the 13 markets. Szegedi sees potential in India and in the women’s market: in the former, the free trade agreement between Bern and New Delhi helps the brands; in the latter, products and the shopping experience must be designed from the outset with female customers in mind. ## Pressure Along the Supply Chain The problem isn’t limited to the brands that sell the finished watch. If volumes decline, suppliers must maintain their machinery, skilled workforce, and know-how at a level that ensures sufficient utilization. A higher final price does not automatically translate this need into a proportional profit for component manufacturers. The difference between a luxury good and the industrial labor required to produce it is at the heart of Szegedi’s warning.
> “A manufacturer of high-precision screws doesn’t earn ten times as much just because its screws end up in a watch that costs ten times as much.”
For those living in Switzerland, the price scale helps explain why demand doesn’t react in the same way. Someone considering a purchase of 80,000 or 100,000 francs may still go ahead with it even when price takes on a different role. Those who have to save up for a watch costing 1,500 or 2,000 francs are much more sensitive to inflation and the rising cost of living. To display this information, use costo della vita in Svizzera; for a price expressed in francs, use comparatore CHF/EUR alongside it.
### Brand, Origin, and New Buyers The reduced importance attributed to the country of origin does not mean that “Swiss Made” has lost all value. According to Szegedi, it remains an important seal of quality, especially for more affordable watches. However, other countries have caught up in terms of quality and design. For premium products, consumer trust depends more on the brand name, to the extent that some manufacturers are consciously choosing not to use the “Swiss Made” designation.
The two emerging markets highlighted by the expert have distinct characteristics. In India, the free trade agreement makes sales more attractive, while large jewelry chains are investing in store infrastructure. The country, however, is not simply the next China. In the women’s market, on the other hand, demand cannot be captured by simply scaling down a men’s model: what’s needed is a product and a sales experience designed from the outset for female customers.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare CHF-EUR exchange options and banks for cross-border workers. ## A Practical Framework for Analyzing the Industry The source provides a practical framework for analyzing the industry without confusing the product’s price with the strength of the industrial base. Anyone evaluating a purchase, a supplier, or a market can follow these steps.
1. Define the price range. Place the watch between 1,000 and 3,000 francs, or distinguish between a purchase of 1,500 or 2,000 francs and one of 80,000 or 100,000 francs. The comparison changes because the reaction to price, inflation, and the cost of living changes.
2. Check the price-to-performance ratio. The country of origin remains a mark of quality, especially for lower-priced models, but other countries have caught up in terms of design and quality. Therefore, it’s not enough to rely solely on the “Swiss Made” label.
3. Consider the industrial side. For a supplier, what matters are production volumes, machinery utilization, skilled labor, and know-how. Diversification into jewelry or medical technology is a path many are pursuing, but not everyone can follow it.
4. Evaluate India with caution. The low- and mid-range segments have potential; a Swiss watch can be a status symbol and a way to treat oneself. The agreement with Bern and investments by jewelry chains help, but India is not simply the next China.
5. Design for female customers. A women’s watch should not merely be a smaller version of a men’s model, a jewelry watch, or a quartz timepiece intended as a gift. Szegedi points to the product and the sales experience as the starting point.
This framework separates the purchasing decision from production capacity. It also helps avoid confusing a high price with the sustainability of the supply chain: these are related but not equivalent concepts. The framework described by Szegedi focuses on the tensions surrounding volume, purchasing power, and product presentation.

item.title: Part-time work among men is increasing in Switzerland
item.description: Since 2000, the percentage of Swiss men working part-time has doubled, exceeding 20%. Analysis of a study based on data from 2004 to 2020, examining the relationship between cultural norms and career paths.
item.content:encoded:
## At a Glance - Since 2000, the proportion of men working part-time has risen from about 10% to over 20%. - In Switzerland, 40% of the workforce works part-time. - The proportion is 60% among women and 20% among men. - The study analyzes Swiss data from 2004 to 2020.
## Key Facts - Data period → 2004–2020 - Full-time men who wish to reduce their hours → 11.4% annually - Actual transition to part-time work → 9.4% of those who wish to do so - Part-time work in Italy in 2025 → 15.3% of the workforce - European Union average → 17.4% - Part-time work in Switzerland by comparison → 40.9% of the workforce
Since 2000, the proportion of Swiss men working part-time has risen from about 10% to over 20%. This figure represents more than a doubling of the rate—a trend unmatched in most industrialized countries. For men, however, part-time work remains a choice made by a minority.
The current picture shows a stark gender difference. About 40% of the Swiss workforce works part-time: the share reaches 60% among women and stands at around 20% among men. Switzerland thus ranks among the countries with the highest prevalence of part-time work in the OECD.
According to a study by sociologists Jan Müller of the University of Zurich and Youngjoo Cha of Indiana University, the explanation is not solely economic. Deep-rooted cultural norms—which associate male identity with the role of primary breadwinner and total availability for work—also hinder the shift to part-time work.
### The Pathway Analyzed by the Researchers The study does not merely provide a snapshot of those working part-time but analyzes the path leading to this choice. The researchers cross-referenced data from the Swiss Labor Force Survey, the Swiss Household Panel, and other employment databases covering the period 2004–2020.
The results show that each year, 11.4% of men employed full-time develop a desire to switch to a reduced work schedule. Among those who develop this preference, 9.4% actually succeed in transitioning to part-time work.
The study identifies two cultural barriers: the ideal of the worker who is always available and the “breadwinner” model—literally, the man who brings home the bread. For an initial comparison of income, the calcolatore stipendio can be used alongside the national data. The national data becomes clearer when compared with the figures recorded in Italy and the European Union. Switzerland has a much higher prevalence of part-time work, but there remains a marked difference between men and women.
| Indicator | Switzerland | Italy or European Union | |---|---:|---:| | Part-time workers | 40.9% | Italy 15.3%; EU 17.4% | | Women working part-time | 60% | EU 27.5% | | Men employed part-time | 20% | EU 7.8%; Italy 8% |
In 2025, part-time work accounted for approximately 15.3% of the employed population in Italy, compared to the European Union average of 17.4%. The Swiss figure included in the comparison, however, stood at 40.9%. In terms of gender, 27.5% of employed women in the European Union worked part-time, compared with 7.8% of men; for Italian men, the source cites 8%.
### The Sector Matters Less Than Professional Norms For those considering a reduction in working hours, the economic sector is not the only factor to consider. The study does not identify any particular differences between sectors but highlights the influence of professional cultures. Men are more likely to switch to part-time work in occupations where a work-life balance is considered legitimate and compatible with one’s career.
The situation changes in professions where the expectation of total availability dominates. When work is placed at the center of both professional and personal life, and men are viewed as the primary breadwinners of the family, the transition to part-time work remains less common. The difference, therefore, also relates to what is considered normal in the workplace.
The feasibility of part-time work in Switzerland also depends on three characteristics identified by the source. Full-time workweeks are relatively long, approaching 42 hours. High wages often make it possible to reduce the level of employment without completely compromising the family’s standard of living. Part-time contracts generally enjoy protection and stability comparable to those of full-time contracts.
A comparison with Sweden and Norway, however, reveals a different model. In the Scandinavian countries, public policies are designed so that both parents can reduce their working hours. In Switzerland, the prevailing pattern remains one in which it is primarily women who work part-time, while men have only recently begun to follow suit. To better understand the income-related aspects of this choice, see busta paga svizzera.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare CHF-EUR exchange options and banks for cross-border workers. The decision to reduce one's employment level can be structured as a practical process, without turning national percentages into an individual promise. The point is to compare working hours, professional culture, income, and family life.
### 1. Measure the starting point Start with full-time hours. The source describes relatively long working weeks, close to 42 hours. Before considering part-time work, therefore, focus on how much availability the job currently requires and what reduction would have a concrete effect on the balance between private life and professional activity.
### 2. Distinguish desire from possibility The study separates the moment when the preference arises from the actual transition to a reduced employment level. This distinction is also useful on a personal level: wanting more free time and managing to incorporate it into the organization of work are two different steps. The comparison must remain anchored in the job performed and the conditions of the workplace.
### 3. Examine the culture of employment Do not stop at the name of the economic sector. Check whether, in the occupation, work-life balance is considered compatible with career progression or whether the expectation of total availability prevails. According to the research, these are the professional cultures that make the difference in the transition to part-time work.
### 4. Consider income and family together The source identifies high wages and generally stable contracts as factors that make part-time work more feasible in Switzerland. The transition must nevertheless be assessed in relation to the family's standard of living and the economic role assigned to each parent. To complement this comparison, costo della vita in Svizzera can be used, without separating the choice of working hours from the family's needs.
The final comparison must bring together the desired employment level, compatibility with career progression, and workplace culture. To estimate the transition from full-time to part-time work, use calcolatore stipendio.

item.title: Artificial intelligence: two out of three Swiss companies use it
item.description: In the first quarter of 2026, AI is being used for recruitment. Seventy-two percent of Swiss companies report a positive return on investment.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - First quarter 2026 data: AI in about two out of three Swiss companies - 72% of companies using AI see a positive return - Systems verify experience, skills, and geographical availability - Experts call for transparency and human oversight
## Key facts - Source → RTS, based on Manpower data - Period → first quarter of 2026 - Adoption → about two out of three Swiss companies - Return on investment → positive for 72% of Swiss companies using AI - Initial phases → verification of experience, skills, and geographical availability - Benefits → team productivity, activity planning, and staff training
Manpower data for the first quarter of 2026 indicates that approximately two out of three Swiss companies were using artificial intelligence in human resources activities. This figure is reported by RTS based on data from Manpower, presented in the source as one of the leading operators in the recruitment sector.
The primary goal is to quickly manage the high volume of applications that can be received for a position. Some systems are used in the early stages of selection: they can verify essential requirements such as professional experience, required skills, and geographical availability. The final decision, according to a statement released by Alliance Care in Bern, will be made on October 14 by the Care Council and the Delegates’ Assembly. Bankruptcy and dissolution are therefore the committee’s proposal, while the final decision rests with the aforementioned governing bodies.
The crisis has been ongoing for months. In June, Alliance Care laid off 17 of its 91 employees. The Swiss Nurses Association (ASI), which initiated the project, has supported the organization through loans.
### The Goal and the Membership Crisis

This mismatch also extends to resources: the range of services offered and the number of staff far exceed revenue. An external analysis concluded that the organization can no longer be restructured.
The project is thus described in terms of two interconnected aspects: the desire to provide the sector with a unified voice and the difficulty of sustaining the organization with sufficient revenue relative to the services provided and the number of staff. The gap between the goal and the level of participation is one of the central themes of the communication.

item.title: Parental Leave: 112,517 Signatures Submitted in Bern
item.description: The initiative for 18 weeks of parental leave has reached the necessary signatures. The proposal aims for equality between parents and fair compensation.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief
- Over 110,000 signatures for 18 weeks of parental leave - 112,517 authenticated signatures delivered to Bern - The proposal provides for the same duration for both mothers and fathers - 100,000 signatures required within 18 months
## Key facts
- Proposal → «Strong society and economy thanks to parental leave» - Demand → «fair and compensated» leave at birth - Signatures → 112,517 authenticated signatures - Threshold → 100,000 signatures within 18 months - Location → Federal Chancellery in Bern - Supporters → The Centre, The Greens, GLP, SP, EVP, FDP, Alliance F and Travail.Suisse - Current situation → 14 weeks for mothers, 2 for fathers
The collection of signatures for an 18-week parental leave, equal for mothers and fathers, has formally succeeded. Today, the promoters deposited 112,517 authenticated signatures at the Federal Chancellery in Bern.
The popular initiative is titled «Strong society and economy thanks to parental leave (Initiative for family leave)». It is supported by representatives from The Centre, The Greens, GLP, SP, EVP, and FDP, as well as Alliance F and Travail.Suisse.
The alliance spoke of strong support from the population. To succeed, a popular initiative requires 100,000 signatures within 18 months of the official publication of the text in the Federal Gazette.
### The constitutional demand
The proposed amendment concerns the Constitution. The text calls for a «fair and compensated» parental leave at the birth of a child and aims to promote de facto equality between the sexes, allowing both parents to pursue gainful employment.
Mothers and fathers should therefore benefit from an identical duration. The promoters also request that the leave be non-transferable and that, in principle, it may be taken alternately for a maximum of one-quarter of the total duration.
Regarding compensation, the text refers to the principles applicable to those performing military or civil service. The minimum amount and financing should be defined on that basis, while the benefit should increase progressively up to 100% for lower wages.
The reference point begins with the current situation described in the source: mothers in gainful employment are entitled to 14 weeks of compensation. In 2020, the people approved two weeks for fathers, which were introduced at the beginning of 2021.
The promoters thus reiterate an issue that has been debated in Switzerland for years: the need to introduce paid leave for both parents. In their view, Switzerland remains among the developed countries with the worst conditions for parental leave in international comparison. Today's filing thus brings together a request regarding duration, a rule on time-sharing, and a criterion for financial support. ## What the Proposed Model Would Entail
The relevant comparison for a family is between the durations currently specified by the source and those required by the initiative. It is not simply a matter of adding weeks: the text links the duration to equality between parents and also establishes how the period should be used.
| Situation | Specified Duration | Eligible Recipients | |---|---|---| | Mothers today | 14 weeks of benefits | Mothers who are employed | | Fathers today | 2 weeks, introduced in early 2021 | Fathers | | Proposal | 18 weeks, with the same duration | Mothers and fathers |
### The time would not be freely transferable
The non-transferability clause must be read in conjunction with the total duration: the text does not describe leave that is freely transferable between parents. Alternating leave is permitted, but in principle not exceeding one-quarter of the total duration. For those planning the period after birth, decisions would therefore concern both the individual duration and the timing of the alternation.
The allowance also follows a specific criterion. The minimum amount and funding should be based on the principles governing the allowance for military or civil service. Furthermore, the benefit should increase progressively until it reaches 100% for the lowest wages. The wage component would therefore become a variable to be considered alongside the rules on duration. To understand the structure of compensation, one can consult the guide to busta paga svizzera, without confusing it with a calculation of the allowance provided for by the initiative.
The promoters cite international comparisons as the rationale for the proposal. The source states that Switzerland ranks among the developed countries with the worst conditions, but it does not provide a ranking nor does it name other countries. The practical analysis must therefore focus on the explicit differences between the current system and the proposed model.
For families, the key difference is the equal duration of leave granted to mothers and fathers. For working individuals, however, other factors also matter, such as the non-transferability of the leave, the limit on alternating leave, and the progressive nature of the allowance. These are distinct elements: the duration does not replace the rules governing how the leave is taken, and those rules do not, on their own, determine the financial amount.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the net salary calculator and the CHF-EUR exchange comparator. ## How to Read the Dossier Without Confusing the Proposal with the Current Situation
The source allows for a practical review in just a few steps. Above all, it helps distinguish between what the proponents are requesting and what is described as already in effect, without attributing a broader meaning to the submission of signatures than is indicated.
### Five steps for those following the initiative
1. Identify the text. The full name is “A Strong Society and Economy Thanks to Parental Leave (Family Leave Initiative).” The key point to note is that it proposes a constitutional amendment to provide leave upon the birth of a child.
2. Check the duration and who is eligible. The proposal calls for 18 weeks, with the same duration for both mothers and fathers. This provision should be distinguished from the current durations indicated by the source.
3. Verify the rules for taking leave. The leave should be non-transferable and, in principle, shared between parents for no more than one-quarter of the total duration. These two conditions should be considered alongside the duration.
4. Examine the allowance separately. The text links the minimum amount and funding to the principles applicable to military or civilian service and provides for a gradual increase up to 100% for the lowest wages. It is not appropriate to interpret this description as a uniform amount for everyone.
5. Place the submission within the context of the procedure. The proponents submitted 112,517 certified signatures to the Federal Chancellery in Bern; the source specifies a threshold of 100,000 signatures within 18 months of publication in the Federal Gazette and formally deems the signature drive successful. The deadline mentioned therefore pertains to the signature collection.
For a family planning the birth of a child, this framework prevents automatically adding up the current durations or assuming the requested model is already in place. For working individuals, it helps keep three elements separate: duration, the possibility of alternating work and leave, and the allowance criteria. This distinction makes it easier to compare the current situation with the proposed legislation.

ZURICH – 68% of the more than 1,000 respondents said they oppose a tax on foods containing sugar, salt, or fat. The responses were collected between March and May by Gfs.Bern for the 13th edition of a survey sponsored by the Soft Drink Information Group.

Two reasons were cited against the tax: the greater burden on poorer people and the belief that the tax would not change eating habits. The call for government intervention remains strong. Seventy-six percent consider the measures taken so far to prevent obesity to be insufficient.

Support rises when the focus shifts to prevention and education. Ninety percent favor programs for at-risk groups and joint initiatives with the private sector. This list does not authorize the interpretation of any figure as a guaranteed savings amount: a deductible, on its own, does not determine the applicable premium. The correct interpretation involves considering the deductible in conjunction with the premium for the Basel-Stadt region and the specific insurance situation in question.
A second element is the premium reduction. This is a cantonal subsidy, not an item defined as a federal tax or payroll tax. For the Canton of Basel-Stadt, the issue must therefore be addressed at the cantonal level, while the LAMal remains the mandatory insurance for residents.
The LAMal e cassa malati guide serves to keep three questions separate: which coverage is mandatory, which adult deductible is being considered, and how to account for the cantonal subsidy. Without an official amount for the year in question, it is incorrect to use a generic figure to describe the premium in Basel-Stadt. ## The comparison that matters in the budget
The practical comparison in Basel-Stadt starts with separating four elements: area, deductible, premium and subsidy. If they are mixed together, the result does not make clear how much health insurance really affects the cost of living. The practical rule is simple: use only the relevant canton and region for the calculation, then note the selected adult deductible and treat the premium reduction separately.
| Item | Function in the comparison | |---|---| | Canton and region | define the geographic scope of the premium | | Adult deductible | identifies one of the six prescribed levels | | LAMal premium | is a per-capita expense | | Premium reduction | is a cantonal subsidy |
The table does not replace an official amount, but it avoids two common errors. The first is to use the premium of a different region or canton as a reference for Basel-Stadt. The second is to add or subtract the subsidy as if it were a salary deduction. LAMal is not a salary contribution: the comparison should be based on the per-capita premium and the cantonal reduction, keeping the two aspects separate.
This separation also helps avoid confusing insurance, taxation and social security. AFC/ESTV concerns direct federal tax and VAT; cantonal administrations manage the cantonal and municipal levels of taxation. UFAS/BSV concerns social security, including AVS/AI/LPP, and does not set taxes; UST/BFS produces statistics and does not set tax rates. These are distinct domains from that of choosing LAMal.
In the overall budget, the premium should therefore be considered alongside the other expenses, without converting it into a percentage of the salary. AVS/AHV and LPP/BVG also belong to the language of social security and salary contributions, whereas the LAMal premium remains per capita. To track the effect on costo della vita in Svizzera, it is advisable to record the item separately; for social security, one can consult the previdenza AVS e LPP guide.
The result is a more cautious comparison: it does not promise savings in the absence of verified amounts, but makes the difference between premium, deductible and subsidy in the Canton of Basel-Stadt clear.

The operational process can be structured without automatically transferring rules from other cantons. For those who need to arrange coverage in Basel-Stadt, five steps bring together the deadline, territory and budget.
1. Set the arrival date. LAMal must be taken out within three months of arrival for those resident in Switzerland. The deadline should be noted before comparing options, because the insurance obligation comes before choosing the deductible.
2. Identify the premium scope. The calculation must refer to the applicable canton and region. Do not use as a basis a figure referring to another territory: premiums are not a uniform national value.
3. Compare adult deductibles. Record separately CHF 300, CHF 500, CHF 1'000, CHF 1'500, CHF 2'000 and CHF 2'500. The comparison remains clear only if each amount is linked to the offer and region considered.
4. Keep the premium reduction separate. It is a cantonal subsidy. In the verification for Basel-Stadt, it must be considered as a separate item from the per-capita premium, taxes and salary contributions. The available information does not allow this check to be replaced with a threshold or amount valid for everyone.
5. Close the monthly budget. Add LAMal expenditure to the overall cost-of-living item, but do not include it among IFD, VAT, AVS/AHV or LPP/BVG: the nature of the premium is different. If alternative models are presented, record for each the premium, region, deductible and any indicated reduction, without adding conditions not reported.
This framework makes it possible to understand where to stop when a data point is missing: figures are not invented, criteria from other cantons are not imported and the cantonal reduction is not confused with a salary deduction. item.description: An international conference organized by the Swiss Confederation on de-escalation in cyberspace is taking place in Zug, focusing on preventive diplomacy, the OSCE, and artificial intelligence.
item.content:encoded:
## At a Glance - The Swiss Confederation promotes de-escalation in cyberspace - Conference held yesterday and today at the Theater Casino in Zug - The initiative takes place during Switzerland’s OSCE Chairmanship - Schütz calls for human verification of artificial intelligence results

The Theater Casino in Zug is hosting the international conference through which the Swiss Confederation is promoting de-escalation in cyberspace. The event is described in the source as an initiative taking place yesterday and today, Wednesday, during Switzerland’s chairmanship of the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE). The two-day event showcases Swiss diplomacy in the cyber realm, following recent events that have highlighted how the virtual world can become a source of tension between countries.
Martin Pfister opened the proceedings yesterday. In his remarks, he emphasized the importance of preventive diplomacy to build trust and of mediation to ease tensions, including in the digital world. The conference thus combines the theme of cyber security with the diplomatic tools already referenced in the opening remarks.
### The Cases Cited and the Proposed Response
Cyberattacks, espionage operations, and artificial intelligence that spirals out of control form the backdrop for the discussion. Florian Schütz, director of the Federal Office for Cybersecurity, cited two cases: artificial intelligence that covertly infiltrates Australian government websites and a false report by U.S. intelligence agencies that creates tensions with China. For Schütz, these incidents demonstrate the limitations of artificial intelligence.
> “This means that humans must verify the results, but it also means that security mechanisms are needed,” Schütz told SRF on the sidelines of the conference.
The director then referred to the confidence-building measures agreed upon by OSCE member states. The next question is how to implement them amid increasingly intense geopolitical tensions and to what extent countries are willing to share the information necessary for defense operations. ## What This Means at the National Level
The supplied text does not mention new legislation, a deadline or a procedure for residents, workers, businesses or administrations. The verifiable national implication must therefore be sought in the Confederation's public position: use preventive diplomacy and mediation to build trust and ease tensions, including digital ones, within the framework of Switzerland's OSCE Chairmanship.
This reading avoids attributing an administrative effect to the conference that the text does not announce. The practical point is to distinguish what is presented as a principle from what remains an open question: human verification and security are described as necessary; applying the confidence-building measures and sharing information for defense remain to be assessed amid geopolitical tensions.
### Four Dimensions to Keep Separate
| Dimension | Indication in the source | |---|---| | Preventive diplomacy | building trust | | Mediation | easing tensions in the digital world | | Artificial intelligence | human verification of results and security mechanisms | | Defense operations | assessing how much necessary information to share |
The combination of these four dimensions shows the nature of the proposal. Schütz's position places human verification and security mechanisms at the center, while the two cases mentioned at the conference show, respectively, the risk of covert access and that of false information capable of fuelling tensions.
